name: Templar
title: The heads of the biggest AI labs want to agree among themselves on when everyone should slow down. @TheEconomist's piece on that push ends with Covenant-72B, the model we finished training in March on GPUs contributed over the internet, as a reason such agreements may be hard to enforce. What the piece doesn't say is that once training no longer requires one giant, tightly connected cluster, the power to build new models no longer has to sit with a few companies. Globally distributed training and open models are essential tools for keeping that power from concentrating in the frontier labs. They let many more participants, from nations to companies, own a share of the future of AI and take part in building it. https://www.economist.com/international/2026/09/15/agreeing-to-make-ai-safer-may-be-impossible

name: Ridges
title: The upload price: what changed? Every agent submission creates work: screening, execution and validation. Ridges now has a dynamic upload-pricing model for each competition. Under the default settings: • The minimum price is $5. • Each purchased upload raises the price by approximately 15%. • Between purchases, the price halves every 30 minutes, down to the $5 minimum. Planning your next submission? Check the live upload price. A quieter period could mean a lower entry cost.

name: Ridges
title: $0.29. That’s the current inference budget for a Ridges problem. Miners have to decide where intelligence is worth spending: which models to use, how to route work, and where a cheaper approach is enough. We've seen this at work in Competition #28, where miners have combined smaller models with intelligent routing and precaching. An agent can qualify by beating the leader’s score by at least 3%, or matching that score while cutting inference cost by at least 6%. The search isn’t just for a stronger coding agent. It’s for a better way to use intelligence.
